name: Marks & Spencer
furFreeNote: Bans farmed fur (fox, sable, mink, chinchilla, rabbit) and also bans angora, yak, camel fibre and kangaroo leather.
sellsNote: Wool must be non-mulesed under its own Responsible Wool Sourcing Policy; down must not come from live-plucked or foie-gras-linked birds.

name: Next
furFreeNote: Fur-free since joining the Fur Free Retailer programme in 2010, and also bans angora and exotic skins (alligator, crocodile, lizard, ostrich, snake) outright.
sellsNote: Leather is cattle/sheep only, with no veal-crate calves; wool must be non-mulesed merino; down must meet the Responsible Down Standard or equivalent.

name: ASOS
furFreeNote: One of the stricter mainstream policies on paper - bans all fur (including Mongolian lamb fur and karakul lambskin), plus angora, exotic skins, down, silk, cashmere and mohair outright.
sellsNote: Leather is limited to cow, buffalo, sheep, goat or pig as a by-product of meat production, with no juvenile or wild-caught animals; wool must not come from mulesing farms.

name: Primark
furFreeNote: Bans all real/farmed fur and bans angora and skins from CITES/IUCN-listed or wild-caught species.
sellsNote: Leather is meant to be a meat-industry by-product from Leather Working Group-certified tanneries where possible; wool must be non-mulesed; down must meet the Responsible Down Standard or IDFL Down Standard.

name: John Lewis
furFreeNote: Explicitly won't accept angora or fur under its Animal Welfare Standard, and bans reptile leather and other exotic skins.
sellsNote: Leather, wool and down are all accepted categories under its Five Provisions framework, each with its own sourcing conditions, but none are banned outright.

sources.label: John Lewis Partnership animal welfare policy

name: H&M
furFreeNote: Bans fur (mink, fox, rabbit, sable, karakul lamb, chinchilla, raccoon dog) and bans angora and all exotic/wild-animal skins.
sellsNote: Leather is cow, buffalo, sheep, goat or pig only, with no fetal or newborn lambskin; wool has targeted full Responsible Wool Standard certification; down must meet the Responsible Down Standard.

name: Zara (Inditex)
furFreeNote: Fur-free as a Fur Free Retailer programme member, and banned angora after 2013-14 campaigns, phasing out mohair by 2020.
sellsNote: Leather comes only from animals raised for food, not solely for hide; wool sourcing bans mulesing. Inditex's public materials page doesn't explicitly confirm a policy on exotic skins or down, so I'm not assuming either way.

sources.label: Zara ends use of angora wool (Retail Dive)

name: Boohoo
furFreeNote: Self-declared fur-free, and says it doesn't use angora or exotic animal skin.
sellsNote: Still uses leather, down and wool, and reviewers (Good On You) describe its 2025 sourcing targets as loosely worded, without tracing animal-derived materials back to the first production stage the way some competitors do.
controversy: Boohoo has a documented, repeated history of real fur mislabelled as faux fur. A 2017 Sky News / Humane Society International UK investigation found real fox, rabbit, chinchilla and mink fur sold as "faux" at Boohoo and several other UK retailers. Separately, the UK Advertising Standards Authority upheld a complaint against boohoo.com in January 2019 after lab testing showed a jumper's "faux fur" pom-pom was real rabbit fur; Boohoo called it a supplier error and the ad was withdrawn. Worth knowing this has happened more than once, not just a single slip.

sources.label: Good On You: How Ethical Is Boohoo?
